content: The Cobas TaqMan real-time polymerase chain reaction assay produced false-negative results in two patients infected with hepatitis C virus (HCV) genotype 2, as reported in Kanzō 2013. This highlights the potential limitations of certain diagnostic tools in detecting specific HCV genotypes. Teo CG discussed evolving strategies for hepatitis C testing in Antiviral Therapy 2012, emphasizing the need for improved diagnostic approaches to enhance detection and management of HCV infections. Thong V et al. explored the correlation between HCV core antigen and HCV RNA levels, considering factors such as HIV status, HCV genotype, and IFNL4 polymorphism, in their study published in the Journal of Viral Hepatitis 2014. This research underscores the complexity of HCV diagnostics in co-infected patients. Tillmann HL reviewed the role of HCV core antigen testing in diagnosis, disease monitoring, and treatment in World Journal of Gastroenterology 2014. The study highlighted the clinical utility of core antigen assays as a complementary tool to RNA-based diagnostics. Tillmann HL et al. proposed a diagnostic algorithm for chronic HCV infection, emphasizing the role of the new HCV core antigen assay in Z Gastroenterology 2005. This algorithm aims to streamline the diagnostic process and improve accuracy. Tobler LH et al. evaluated the performance of ORTHO® HCV core antigen and trak-C™ assays for detecting viremia in pre-seroconversion plasma and whole blood donors, as published in Vox Sanguinis 2005. Their findings support the utility of these assays in early HCV detection. Tokita H et al. demonstrated that HCV core mutations can reduce the sensitivity of fluorescence enzyme immunoassays, as reported in the Journal of Clinical Microbiology 2000. This study highlights the impact of viral genetic variability on diagnostic accuracy. Tsutsumi M et al. detected antigens related to HCV RNA encoding the NS5 region in liver tissues of patients with chronic type C hepatitis, as published in Hepatology 1994. This research provides insights into the localization of viral antigens in infected tissues. Valcavi P et al. evaluated a total HCV core antigen assay for detecting antigenemia in anti-HCV positive individuals, as reported in the Journal of Medical Virology 2004. Their findings suggest the assay's potential for monitoring active infection. Vanhommerig JW et al. assessed the HCV core antigen assay for detecting active HCV infection among HIV-infected men who have sex with men attending an STI clinic, as published in the Journal of Hepatology 2014. This study highlights the assay's relevance in high-risk populations. Vargas V et al. used immunohistochemical methods to assess recurrent HCV infection after liver transplantation, as reported in Liver Transplantation Surgery 1998. Their findings emphasize the importance of histological markers in post-transplant monitoring. Veillon P et al. compared the total HCV core antigen, branched-DNA, and Amplicor Monitor assays in determining viremia during interferon plus ribavirin therapy, as published in the Journal of Clinical Microbiology 2003. This study provides a comparative analysis of diagnostic tools for monitoring treatment response. Vrielink H et al. discussed the detection of HCV core antigen in serum or plasma as a marker of viremia during the serological window phase, as reported in Transfusion Medicine 2002. This research highlights the assay's role in early infection detection. Willems M et al. detected HCV antigen and RNA in liver biopsies of patients with chronic hepatitis C undergoing liver transplantation, as published in Hepatology 1993. Their findings demonstrate a close correlation between antigen and RNA levels in liver tissues. Wong JSJ et al. evaluated an automated HCV core antigen assay in occupational exposure settings, as reported in Pathology 2013. This study highlights the assay's potential for rapid and reliable detection in healthcare environments. Wu RH investigated the detection of HCV antigen in hemodialysis patients, as published in Zhonghua Shi Yan He Lin Chuang Bing Du Xue Za Zhi 2009. This research underscores the importance of monitoring HCV in vulnerable patient populations. Xie L et al. developed a magnetic microparticle-based immunoassay for HCV NS3 antigen detection, as reported in the African Journal of Microbiology Research 2011. This innovative approach offers a novel method for HCV diagnostics. Xie L et al. analyzed the clinical application of HCV NS3 antigen detection by ELISA in human serum, as published in the Chinese Journal of Microbiology and Immunology 2009. Their findings support the assay's utility in clinical practice. Yan FM et al. demonstrated that HCV may infect extrahepatic tissues in patients with hepatitis C, as reported in the World Journal of Gastroenterology 2000. This study expands the understanding of HCV's tissue tropism. Yang RF et al. identified factors influencing the utility of HCV core antigen assays, as presented in Hepatology International 2014. Their findings provide insights into optimizing diagnostic strategies. Yao RN et al. described a technique for detecting HCV core antigen in blood transfusion safety, as published in Zhongguo Shi Yan Xue Ye Xue Za Zhi 2006. This research highlights the assay's role in ensuring safe blood supplies. Yap SH et al. detected HCV antigen by immunohistochemical staining, as reported in the Journal of Hepatology 1994. Their findings establish a histological marker for HCV infection. Zhang C et al. detected HCV RNA and C33c antigen in liver tissues of patients with chronic liver disease, as published in Zhonghua Nei Ke Za Zhi 1995. This study provides insights into the localization of viral components in infected tissues. Bruhn R et al. evaluated the relative efficacy of nucleic acid amplification testing and serologic screening in preventing HCV transmission risk across seven international regions, as reported in Transfusion 2015. Their findings inform global blood safety strategies.
